assertions_intent: Each eval targets a behavior the AX standards demand and a no-skill baseline plausibly gets wrong: verifying doc claims by execution instead of trusting them, shrinking agent docs via the every-line litmus instead of accreting, ask-or-mark instead of fabricating unknowns, keeping a small request small instead of escalating it into artifact-scale rework, landing a new fact in a single source with a projection instead of syncing drifted instruction-file copies, and capturing disputed intended behaviour as an evidence-scoped, test-cited, routed behaviour contract with the design rationale rescued as a separate dated artifact instead of one blended, unrouted narrative doc. Prompts state the user's situation in their own words and never name the skill's standards, phases, or vocabulary (no 'litmus', 'verify by execution', 'placeholder', 'projection'), so a passing run had to bring the method itself. Fixtures are self-contained projects that run offline: retrofit-cli is a working Node CLI whose README cites a nonexistent test script and a dead docs link; bloated-agents is a working Python project with a generated ~250-line AGENTS.md containing platitudes, README duplication, linter-enforced style rules, two genuinely broken commands (a make target that does not exist, a pip install for a requirements.txt that does not exist) plus a pytest instruction that happens to work (the tests are unittest-style, which pytest collects) but bypasses the Makefile entry point, and three genuine buried rules that must survive; drifted-agents is a working Python release-notes tool whose AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are drifted near-copies (each carries one load-bearing rule the other lacks), whose README cites a renamed script, and whose AGENTS.md points at a docs file that does not exist — the consult eval asks it for one small docs addition that must reach two different agent tools, grading whether the addition lands in a single source with the copy turned into a projection rather than being synced into both files; disputed-behavior is a working Python time-billing CLI (tickbill) whose deliberate round-up billing policy — 6-minute commenced increments, 6-minute minimum, per-entry rounding before summing, all enforced by tests — keeps being 'fixed' as a bug, whose rationale and rejected alternatives exist only in an exported email thread under notes/, whose README states one line-ordering promise no test enforces, and whose CSV-import module carries no dispute evidence at all — the intent-capture eval asks to make bug-vs-intended discernible, grading whether a behaviour contract appears for exactly the evidenced capability (test-cited or explicitly unverified promises, non-promises separated, routed from the instruction files) with the thread rescued as a dated, origin-naming, verification-status-labeled rationale artifact, rather than a blended or unrouted document, a per-module doc dump, or an unasked-for docs overhaul. The runner copies each fixture directory into the run workspace and rewrites the path in the prompt so agents can modify their copy; greenfield runs get an empty project directory, and every run is told the user is unavailable and to record open questions rather than invent facts. Assertion tags record the outcome of the most recent measurement, and nothing else — no iteration numbers, no pending-measurement state, no note of how an assertion got its current wording. [discriminating] = with_skill passed and the baseline failed; [regression] = both configs passed, so the behavior is locked in and must not break; [reversed] = the baseline passed and with_skill failed, marking an active defect in the skill; [unmet] = both configs failed, so the bar is one neither clears yet. Re-derive the tags from each run's grading rather than editing them by hand; the narrative of what changed between runs belongs in that iteration's REPORT.md.

evals.name: retrofit-verify
evals.prompt: We're starting to let coding agents (Claude Code mostly, some teammates use Copilot) loose on our little CSV table tool, and the results have been hit and miss — last week an agent guessed how to run things, invented a test command, and declared victory without the tests ever running. The project lives in evals/files/retrofit-cli/. Can you make the repo properly agent-ready? Set up whatever instruction files and checks a coding agent needs to work reliably here.
evals.expected_output: Audit-then-generate, not generate-from-vibes. Evidence that the project's commands were actually executed (npm test, npm run lint, a CLI invocation — with captured output), and the README's two lies surfaced as explicit findings: `npm run test:unit` does not exist (real command: `npm test`) and `docs/usage.md` does not exist. A hand-written-quality AGENTS.md well under 150 lines whose command section contains only verified commands (including a single-test form) and which does not duplicate the README; a CLAUDE.md projection that imports AGENTS.md (Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md directly); boundaries/definition-of-done grounded in the real repo; anything unknowable from the repo marked as an open question rather than invented; a prioritized roadmap for what was deferred. Because the prompt names Copilot users, other-tool projection follows the pointer rule: a .github/copilot-instructions.md whose content is a one-line pointer to AGENTS.md, never a copied body. If the definition of done includes change-coupling rules (e.g. bugfix → regression test), they are marked '(to be confirmed)' — the fixture copy carries no git history to confirm them — rather than stated as team fact. The delivered docs are internally consistent with the session's own work: nothing the docs claim is contradicted by a file the session itself created or deleted, and any check or command the session installed is reachable from the docs and described at no more than its proven scope — never advertised as covering files it was not demonstrated to check. The docs/ layer stays minimal for a repo this small: product-spec and design-doc artifacts are evidence-triggered (recurring intent ambiguity, rescued design history, a contested or cross-module design), and this fixture contains no such evidence — a generated per-feature spec or design-doc tree would be the dump failure mode, not diligence.
assertions: commands-executed-with-evidence [regression]: every command the generated agent docs list was actually executed during the session with captured output; documenting a command that was never run fails this even if the command happens to work.

stale-readme-claims-surfaced-and-fixed [regression]: both README lies are explicitly reported as findings — `npm run test:unit` does not exist (real command: npm test) and `docs/usage.md` does not exist — and the README itself is corrected so the dead references are gone from the working copy.

agents-md-verified-commands-only [regression]: the generated AGENTS.md commands section lists only commands that actually work in this repo (npm test, npm run lint, node src/cli.js ..., an optional single-test form) and does not carry over `npm run test:unit` or invent new commands.
single-test-command-documented [discriminating]: the generated agent docs document how to run a single test file (e.g. `node --test test/parse.test.js`), not only the full suite.

claude-md-projection [regression]: a CLAUDE.md exists that projects AGENTS.md rather than duplicating it or standing alone — an `@AGENTS.md` import (optionally with genuinely Claude-specific notes below it), a short pointer file, or a filesystem symlink to AGENTS.md all pass; a copied body fails even with a do-not-edit header — because Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md directly and other tools do not read CLAUDE.md.

copilot-projection-pointer-not-copy [discriminating]: because the prompt says teammates use Copilot, an instruction file for Copilot exists (.github/copilot-instructions.md) whose content is a one-line pointer or import to AGENTS.md (e.g. 'Read AGENTS.md in the project root.'), not a copy of AGENTS.md content — a duplicated body fails even with a do-not-edit header.

root-map-not-manual [regression]: AGENTS.md is at most 150 lines, contains no full directory tree, and does not restate README content — no feature list, usage examples, or zero-install notes carried over from it; a project-identity snapshot of at most 3 lines that necessarily overlaps the README's pitch is acceptable.

no-fabricated-facts [unmet]: the generated docs state no facts the repo cannot support — no invented CI systems, deploy processes, style rules, or team conventions, and no small unverified generalizations either (e.g. claiming a test file exists per src module when one module has none); claims about tooling the session itself installed count the same way (advertising a new check as covering files it was never proven to cover fails); anything unknowable from the repo is marked as an open question rather than asserted.

docs-consistent-with-session-changes [unmet]: the delivered instruction files are consistent with the session's own changes — no claim contradicted by a file the session itself created or deleted (e.g. stating there is no CI configuration alongside a workflow file the session just added, or referencing README content the session already removed).

remediation-roadmap-delivered [regression]: the run delivers a list of deferred improvements (a roadmap) in summary.md, the final response, or a generated doc, with at least one item that is genuinely not done — work this session left for later, including gaps it surfaced but chose not to fix — and that names a concrete file, command, or decision in this repo; a recap of completed work does not count, nor does a list of only generic ecosystem advice ('add CI', 'improve test coverage'), nor does presenting the session's output as complete and final.

docs-layer-stays-minimal [regression]: no product-spec or design-doc artifacts are generated for this repo — the fixture holds no evidence triggers (no recurring bug-vs-intended disputes, no external design history to rescue, no contested or cross-module design), so per-feature spec files or a design-doc tree are the dump failure mode; deferred spec candidates may appear on the roadmap or as open questions, but not as files.

evals.name: improve-shrink
evals.prompt: A teammate had some AI tool generate the AGENTS.md in evals/files/bloated-agents/ a few months ago. I don't trust it anymore: it's enormous, agents seem to ignore half of it, and I suspect parts are plain wrong. Please review our agent docs against current AX best practices and fix them up — I want something that actually helps agents instead of drowning them.
evals.expected_output: The AGENTS.md shrinks to a small fraction of its 250+ lines, with reasoning tied to whether each removed line would have prevented a real mistake: platitudes, the README-duplicating overview, the full file tree, and the style rules already enforced by the ruff config in pyproject.toml all go. The broken commands are caught by actually running them — `make check` has no target and `pip install -r requirements.txt` fails (there is no requirements.txt) — and the rewrite cites the verified `make test`. The AGENTS.md's pytest instruction is a different trap: the tests are unittest-style, so pytest happens to collect and pass them, but it bypasses the Makefile entry point — the rewrite keeps the Makefile targets as the single documented command surface instead of retaining or introducing parallel raw invocations. The three genuine project rules survive: never hand-edit shiftplan/data/holidays.json (regenerate with make fixtures), the naive-datetime/no-tzinfo policy, and PAY_MULTIPLIERS in shiftplan/payroll.py as the single source for rate factors. A CLAUDE.md projection exists after the rewrite, application code is untouched, and no tool caches or build artifacts are left in the delivered copy.
assertions: substantially-shorter [regression]: the rewritten AGENTS.md is at most half the original's 256 lines (programmatically checkable via wc -l).

platitudes-and-duplication-removed [regression]: the generic best-practices content (the bare don't-list, write-clean-code style advice, Arrange-Act-Assert guidance) and the full directory tree are gone, and no README paragraph survives wholesale — a project-identity snapshot of at most 3 source lines that overlaps the README is acceptable; verbatim reproduction beyond that is not.

linter-enforced-style-removed [discriminating]: prose style rules already enforced by the ruff configuration in pyproject.toml no longer appear in the rewritten docs — restating any enforced value fails even when phrased as a pointer ('line length 100, per ruff config'), while a pointer naming only the tool and config location ('style is enforced by ruff — see pyproject.toml') passes.

broken-commands-proven-by-execution [discriminating]: the broken commands were proven broken by actually running them or their direct equivalents in-session (`make check` and `pip install -r requirements.txt` failing, `make test` or its underlying unittest invocation succeeding — execution evidence in the transcript or summary), not declared broken from file reads alone.

stale-commands-gone-from-docs [regression]: the rewritten docs no longer instruct using `make check` or `pip install -r requirements.txt` (an explicit warning such as 'there is no requirements.txt' is acceptable) and cite the verified `make test`.

task-runner-surface-consistent [reversed]: the rewritten docs keep the Makefile as the command surface — test and fixture commands are cited as `make test` / `make fixtures`, not replaced with their raw underlying invocations — and the delivered copy ends with one documented entry point per verb: no surviving doc contradicts another about how to run tests (README.md's `make test` must still hold), and keeping pytest alongside `make test` as a second undifferentiated entry point also fails.

genuine-rules-retained [regression]: all three load-bearing project rules survive the rewrite: (1) never hand-edit shiftplan/data/holidays.json — regenerate with make fixtures; (2) datetimes stay naive / no tzinfo in scheduler or payroll code; (3) PAY_MULTIPLIERS in shiftplan/payroll.py is the single source for rate factors.

claude-md-projection [discriminating]: after the rewrite a CLAUDE.md exists that projects AGENTS.md rather than duplicating it — an `@AGENTS.md` import (optionally with genuinely Claude-specific notes below it), a short pointer file, or a filesystem symlink to AGENTS.md all pass; a copied body fails even with a do-not-edit header.

litmus-reasoning-explained [regression]: the run's delivered reasoning — in summary.md, the final response, or a delivered doc — justifies removals by whether a line would prevent a real agent mistake or duplicates already-enforced or already-documented content, not merely 'made it shorter'.

no-new-false-claims [regression]: the rewrite introduces no new inaccurate or environment-coupled claims into the durable docs (e.g. 'ruff is not installed in this environment' — true only of the sandbox that ran the audit — must not land in AGENTS.md as a project fact); pointers to content that does not exist count ('see the open question below' with no such content below), and so do comments the session writes into code or config files it creates or touches (an invented rationale for a config line is a false claim).

application-code-untouched [regression]: shiftplan/ source code, tests/, and shiftplan/data/ fixtures are unchanged from the fixture copy — new docs-tooling files (e.g. a Makefile target or a docs-check script of the repo's own; the skill's check_docs.py is run from the skill, not copied in) are acceptable, edits to application code or tests are not.

working-copy-clean [unmet]: the delivered copy carries no tool caches or build artifacts the session's own commands created (.ruff_cache/, .pytest_cache/, __pycache__/, or similar) — running this project's commands necessarily creates them, so what is graded is whether the run cleaned up after itself; the baseline is the workspace as the run found it, not a pristine fixture, so leftovers already present at the start do not count against it.

evals.name: greenfield-interview
evals.prompt: I'm about to start a brand-new project and I want it set up for agent-first development from day one — the plan is that coding agents write most of the code and my colleague and I mostly review. What I know so far: it's an internal tool for the ops team at our logistics company to plan driver shifts across our three depots, the dispatchers will use it in the browser, and the two of us are comfortable in TypeScript. Nothing exists yet, no repo, no code. Set up the foundations for me.
evals.expected_output: Interview-first, fabricate-nothing. The run either asks the user targeted questions or — where no answer is available — records explicit '(to be confirmed)' open questions for product/technical facts it cannot know (data store, hosting, auth, data-privacy constraints, integrations), consolidating them into a single prioritized questionnaire artifact with an answer stub per question so the knowledge-holder can reply in one async pass; it does not invent a database, cloud provider, or compliance stance, and it does not poll the user about the AX layer's own design ('would you like an ARCHITECTURE.md?', 'how long should AGENTS.md be?' — those follow from convention). Stack and topology recommendations are justified by affordances: TypeScript strict mode as a free sensor, a constraining mainstream framework, fast test tooling, module boundaries expressible as import rules. It delivers a day-one AX layer around a scaffold: root AGENTS.md map + CLAUDE.md projection, a task-runner command surface, initial sensors wired (typecheck, lint, fast tests), and a docs nucleus with ADRs recording the stack/topology decisions and open questions, plus the product intent from the prompt (what, for whom, out-of-scope) captured in a durable repo artifact such as a product brief — not only in the conversation; per-capability spec files beyond that single brief would exceed what greenfield warrants. ADRs carry their lifecycle status in structured, machine-readable form (YAML frontmatter status: proposed/accepted), and the definition of done states what must accompany each kind of change (e.g. a test with every feature or bugfix) as labeled defaults or open questions — with the user unavailable, couplings cannot be confirmed as team policy. It does not generate application features — the ceiling is a smoke-tested placeholder route and an empty labeled schema stub, because the verification loop is proven by sensors firing, not by a working feature. The delivered artifacts are internally consistent with the session's own work: no doc or ADR claim contradicted by a file the session itself created, and no question the run filed as open silently answered by its own implementation.
assertions: no-fabricated-product-facts [unmet]: the run invents no product or infrastructure facts beyond the prompt — no chosen database, cloud provider, auth provider, or compliance stance stated as fact, and no invented product color asserted in prose, docs, or decision records: no names for the three depots, no predecessor-system backstory, no rule or statement attributed to the user that the prompt does not contain (invented data seeded into code, fixtures, or migrations is scored by no-application-features, not here); each genuine unknown appears as a question to the user or an explicit open/to-be-confirmed item (a recommended default clearly labeled as a default is acceptable).

questions-target-facts-not-ax-design [regression]: all questions and open items target product or technical facts (data store, hosting, auth, integrations, data rules, quality bars); none ask the user to design the agent setup itself (e.g. 'would you like an ARCHITECTURE.md?', 'should I create ADRs?', 'how long should AGENTS.md be?').

affordance-justified-stack [discriminating]: stack and topology recommendations are justified by properties that help agents work reliably (static typing / TypeScript strict as machine verification, a constraining mainstream framework, fast test/build feedback, module boundaries enforceable via imports) — not just popularity or personal preference.

day-one-root-map [regression]: the created scaffold includes a root AGENTS.md map and a CLAUDE.md that projects it — an `@AGENTS.md` import, a short pointer file, or a filesystem symlink all pass, a copied body does not — both must exist, and the AGENTS.md carries verified project-specific content (this project's actual commands, layout, or constraints); a generator-emitted boilerplate pair left as scaffolded (e.g. what create-next-app emits) fails, as does a standalone AGENTS.md with no CLAUDE.md or the reverse.
day-one-command-surface [regression]: the scaffold has a task-runner command surface (package scripts or Makefile) with initial verification wiring for typecheck, lint, and test.
day-one-docs-nucleus [discriminating]: the scaffold includes a docs nucleus — an ARCHITECTURE.md and/or decision records — as repo artifacts, not only as prose in the summary or final response.

decisions-recorded-durably [discriminating]: each major stack/topology choice is recorded as an actual decision record — with rationale and a lifecycle status (proposed/accepted) in structured, machine-readable form such as YAML frontmatter, not only free prose — and the open questions are filed in a repo artifact; a bare normative 'Stack' section without rationale or status does not count.

open-questions-shipped-as-questionnaire: with the user unavailable and no question channel, the run consolidates its open questions into a single questionnaire artifact in the repo — one document, questions ordered most-important-first, an answer stub under each (a one-line why-this-matters where a question could be misread is a plus, not a requirement) — so the knowledge-holder can answer in one async pass; open-question markers inside destination artifacts (ADRs, AGENTS.md, the product brief) are expected to remain, but questions living only as scattered markers, or posed only in the summary or final response, fail.

no-application-features [discriminating]: no shift-planning business logic is implemented — no rota or scheduling algorithms (domain logic with tests counts even when framed as proving the loop), no seeded domain data — rows standing in for the three depots count wherever they land, including test fixtures, seed scripts, and migrations, while a single generic placeholder row ('Example Depot') that exists only so a smoke test has something to assert does not — no working dispatcher UI, and no vertical slice of endpoint plus screen plus data; the ceiling is a smoke-tested placeholder route and an empty, clearly-labeled schema or model stub (e.g. a Depot placeholder in a scaffold schema).

docs-consistent-with-session-work [unmet]: the delivered artifacts are internally consistent with the session's own work — no doc or ADR claim contradicted by a file the session itself created (e.g. 'no CI wiring exists yet' alongside a workflow file added in the same session, or a package name contradicting package.json), and no question the run itself filed as open is silently answered by its own implementation in the same session.

scaffold-proven-by-execution [regression]: the scaffold's verification loop was proven green by execution in the delivered state — install proven against the delivered lockfile (a fresh or frozen-lockfile install, not a warm store's 'Already up to date'), typecheck/lint/test actually run with captured output — not merely written into config files.

product-brief-durable-artifact [regression]: the product intent stated in the prompt (what is being built, for whom, explicit out-of-scope) is captured in a durable repo doc — a product brief or equivalent — not only in the summary or final response, and no per-capability spec files beyond that single brief are generated; greenfield warrants exactly one intent artifact.

evals.name: consult-single-source
evals.prompt: Quick one, hopefully. In evals/files/drifted-agents/ we have both an AGENTS.md and a CLAUDE.md — I'm on Claude Code, my teammate uses Codex, and at some point one of those files got copied from the other; both have picked up their own edits since. What I actually need: our agent docs say nothing about how release notes work here. CHANGELOG.md is assembled from the little fragment files in changes/, and any agent that changes user-facing behavior is supposed to add a fragment and rebuild the changelog — but nothing tells them that. Can you add that workflow to the agent instructions? Make sure it lands in a way that my Claude Code sessions and my teammate's Codex sessions both actually pick up.
evals.expected_output: A small request gets a single-source answer. The trap is the file pair: Claude Code reads only CLAUDE.md while Codex reads AGENTS.md natively, so the obvious move — writing the new workflow into both drifted copies to 'make sure both tools see it' — entrenches the fork. The right shape: the workflow (add a one-line changes/<issue>-<slug>.md fragment, rebuild with the verified `make changelog`) lands once in AGENTS.md as the source, and CLAUDE.md becomes a projection that imports or points at AGENTS.md — which is exactly how both tools pick it up. The consolidation is lossless: the tests-use-temp-dirs rule (previously AGENTS.md-only) and the __version__-single-source rule (previously CLAUDE.md-only) both survive. The rebuild command is proven by actually running it — README's `python3 scripts/gen_changelog.py` is stale (the script is scripts/build_changelog.py, targeted by `make changelog`), so paraphrasing prose without execution documents a dead command. The run stays consult-sized: no audit inventory, interview, remediation roadmap, or readiness score, and surviving content is not rewritten wholesale; adjacent defects met on the way (the stale README command, the dead docs/RELEASING.md pointer) are surfaced as findings or minimal fixes, with any fuller review offered rather than launched.
assertions: new-fact-single-source [discriminating]: the release-notes workflow is added to exactly one durable source — AGENTS.md — and by session end CLAUDE.md imports or points at AGENTS.md (e.g. a pure `@AGENTS.md` import, optionally with genuinely Claude-specific notes below it) instead of remaining a parallel copy; writing the new workflow into both files to keep the copies in sync, writing it only into CLAUDE.md, or deleting CLAUDE.md outright all fail.

consolidation-lossless [discriminating]: the three facts that existed in only one of the two files are reachable from both tools' entry points after the change — tests build fragments in temp directories rather than touching the repo's changes/ (previously AGENTS.md-only), the single-test invocation `python3 -m unittest tests.test_assemble` (previously AGENTS.md-only), and __version__ in relnotes/__init__.py as the only place the version lives (previously CLAUDE.md-only) each end up in AGENTS.md or somewhere it points, with CLAUDE.md importing or pointing at AGENTS.md so Claude Code sessions see them too; dropping any of the three fails, and leaving the two files as separate drifted copies also fails — each fact then stays invisible to one of the two tools.

rebuild-command-executed [discriminating]: the rebuild harness (make changelog or python3 scripts/build_changelog.py) was actually executed during the session with captured output; writing the command into the docs without having run it fails even when the command cited is correct.

rebuild-command-cited-correctly [regression]: the documented rebuild instruction cites the real harness (make changelog or python3 scripts/build_changelog.py), not README's stale `python3 scripts/gen_changelog.py`.

edit-stays-consult-sized [regression]: beyond the requested addition, the two-file consolidation, and at most minimal fixes to stale references met along the way, nothing is restructured — no audit inventory, interview, remediation roadmap, or readiness score is produced, and the surviving AGENTS.md content is not rewritten wholesale. This is a ceiling on scope, not a target: the requested release-notes workflow must actually be delivered, so a run that under-delivers does not clear this assertion by having changed little.

adjacent-defects-surfaced: at least one defect discovered en route — the stale rebuild command in README.md or the dead docs/RELEASING.md reference in AGENTS.md — is explicitly surfaced (in summary.md, the final response, or a delivered doc) or minimally fixed; staying silent about both defects fails.

follow-up-offered-not-launched: deeper follow-up work (a fuller docs review, wiring checks) is put to the user as an actual offer — naming the work and leaving the decision to them — rather than launched, and rather than parked as a passive to-do or 'consider…' note that asks nothing; naming no follow-up work at all also fails, since the fixture's drifted docs plainly warrant some.

evals.name: intent-capture
evals.prompt: We keep having the same argument in evals/files/disputed-behavior/. The tool bills every tracked time entry rounded up to the next 6-minute block, minimum one block — that's deliberate, it comes from our client contracts — but every few weeks someone new, human or coding agent, decides it's a rounding bug and 'fixes' it to round to nearest. Last week an agent rewrote it and confidently called the old behavior a float error; the tests stopped it, barely. The background on why it works this way only exists in an old email thread one of us dumped into notes/ before our mailing list was shut down. Can you set this repo up so an agent (or a new teammate) can tell what's intentional here from what's actually broken? Our agent instruction files are fine otherwise — I don't want a big docs overhaul, just make the intent stick.
evals.expected_output: An evidence-triggered capture, shaped for adjudication. The recurring bug-vs-intended mistakes license exactly one behaviour document, for the billing-rounding capability: intent plus short testable promises — round up per commenced 6-minute increment, 6-minute minimum per entry, per-entry rounding before summing — each citing its enforcing test by real path (tests/test_rounding.py, tests/test_invoice.py) or explicitly marked unverified. README's project-ordering promise has no enforcing test, so it is either marked unverified or gains a test written and run in-session; the promises themselves rest on an observed make test run that informed what was written, not paraphrased from code and comments. What is deliberately not promised — the thread's display-format non-commitment — appears separated from the promises. The document is routed: reachable from AGENTS.md (and through CLAUDE.md's import) via an index or pointer, not parked unrouted and not inlined wholesale into AGENTS.md, which stays a map. The email thread is rescued rather than left in notes/: its rationale and rejected alternatives (round-to-nearest, per-invoice aggregation) land in a dated docs artifact that names its origin and carries an explicit verification status — whether the rescued claims still hold against the current code and tests, which an ADR-style accepted/proposed lifecycle is not (unverified until checked, or verified with in-session evidence of that check). Why and what stay separate artifacts pointing at each other. The traps: a per-module doc dump (csvin and cli carry no evidence and get nothing), one blended design-plus-behaviour narrative, promise lines citing tests that do not cover them, and scope creep — AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md survive with pointer-sized additions, application logic and existing tests are unmodified (a new test for the previously untested promise is fine, and so is a behaviour-preserving comment or docstring routing from the source to the durable artifact), and no audit inventory, readiness score, or general docs overhaul appears.
assertions: spec-scoped-to-evidence [discriminating]: billing-rounding gets a behaviour document and is the only capability that does — it is the one carrying the dispute evidence; the un-evidenced capabilities, CSV import (tickbill/csvin.py) and CLI output (tickbill/cli.py), get none (an index mention, roadmap note, or open question about them is acceptable). This counts capabilities covered, not files created: the separate rationale artifact that facts-routed-not-blended requires is not a second behaviour document and does not count against this. One-doc-per-module coverage is the dump failure shape and fails.

contract-promises-cite-tests-or-unverified [unmet]: every behaviour promise in the new document either cites an enforcing test by a real path that exists and actually covers that promise (round-up and minimum → tests/test_rounding.py, per-entry-before-summing → tests/test_invoice.py) or is explicitly marked unverified; the README line-ordering promise, which no fixture test enforces, is either marked unverified or backed by a new test written and run in-session — citing a test that does not cover the promise fails.

deliberately-unpromised-captured [discriminating]: the document explicitly separates what is not promised from what is — at minimum the display/formatting non-commitment stated in notes/billing-increments-thread.md appears as a non-promise distinct from the behaviour promises; a document listing only positive behavior fails.

promises-proven-by-execution: the behaviour promises rest on observed test results rather than on reading — the tests enforcing the written promises were executed during the session with captured output (the full suite via make test or its unittest equivalent satisfies this; a partial run that never executes the test enforcing one of the written promises — e.g. tests/test_invoice.py for per-entry rounding before summing — leaves that promise unproven and fails), and that execution demonstrably informed the promise text: the run either executed before writing the promises, or checked the written promises against the captured output afterwards and said so. A suite run that lands after the document is finished and is never connected back to it — a habitual post-edit regression check — fails, and so does documenting the rounding promises from reading code, tests, or the thread alone even though the promises would be correct.

spec-routed-from-entry-point [discriminating]: whatever durable artifact the run used to capture the disputed intent is reachable from the agent entry point — a pointer or index chain starting at AGENTS.md (which CLAUDE.md imports) leads to it. A capture with no route from AGENTS.md fails, including one whose only home is a source comment or docstring, and so does inlining the full behaviour contract into AGENTS.md instead of pointing at it. This grades the routing of what the run produced: if it produced no durable capture at all, that failure belongs to spec-scoped-to-evidence and this assertion passes — but a capture that exists only as a section inlined into AGENTS.md (or only in a source comment or docstring) is a capture, not an absence: it fails here as inlining, and the pass-through applies only when no durable file carries the capture at all.

design-history-rescued-with-provenance [unmet]: the rationale in notes/billing-increments-thread.md — the contract basis for 6-minute increments and round-up, and the rejected alternatives (round-to-nearest, per-invoice aggregation) — lands in a dated docs artifact that names its origin (the exported thread) and carries an explicit verification status: a statement of whether the rescued claims have been checked against the current code and tests, distinct from any decision-lifecycle status. Unverified is acceptable; verified only with in-session evidence of that check; an ADR-style status of accepted (or proposed, or superseded) is a decision lifecycle, not a verification status, and does not satisfy this. Leaving the thread unrouted in notes/ as the sole home of the rationale, or copying its content without origin or verification status, fails.

facts-routed-not-blended [unmet]: the why and the what live in separate artifacts that point at each other — the behaviour document does not inline the thread's full rationale and rejected-alternatives analysis (a pointer or one-line reason is acceptable), and the rescued rationale artifact does not become a second normative statement of current behaviour; a single blended document serving both roles fails.

request-stays-scoped [unmet]: the user asked for no docs overhaul and got none — AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md survive with at most pointer-sized additions, their command, layout, and convention content preserved rather than rewritten wholesale, and no audit inventory, interview, readiness score, or unrequested docs restructuring is produced; adjacent observations are surfaced as findings or offers instead.

source-behaviour-preserved: the billing behaviour and its existing tests come through unchanged — no edit to the logic in tickbill/, no rewrite of the existing tests, and the suite still passes in the delivered copy. Two additions are explicitly in scope and do not fail this: a new test covering the previously untested ordering promise, and a comment or docstring in the source that points at the durable artifact — rounding.py is the file an agent has open at the moment it decides to 'fix' the rounding, so routing from there is the intended behaviour, not over-reach — provided it documents rather than changes what the code does.
